strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: estimating weighted distances when weights become available after compression. The discussion usefully distinguishes this objective from ordinary JL reduction with known weights and related nearest-neighbor methods.

The fourth-root-of-unity construction gives an elegant unbiased estimator. Theorem 3 correctly exploits vanishing first, second, and third moments to isolate the desired weighted squared norm. Linearity of the stored projection permits estimation on vector differences.

The distortion parameter identifies an important limitation caused by poor overlap between input energy and selected features. The experiments illustrate this effect and qualitatively demonstrate improved concentration as the sketch grows.
weaknesses: The central concentration theorem is false. In Theorem 2, take γ=2 and a_(i,j)=1 for every i≠j. Then S=(Σ_i X_i)^2−n, so P[S≥n(n−1)]=2^(1−n), whereas the claimed bound is C₂ exp(−n(n−1)/4). These contradict one another for sufficiently large n, regardless of the dimension-independent constant C₂. Lemma 5 incorrectly replaces even moments by powers of Σa², omitting surviving mixed terms and multiplicities. Consequently, Corollary 1, Lemma 10, and the headline dimension guarantee in Theorem 5 are unsupported. This central correctness failure motivates rejection.

The streaming analysis has a separate proof gap. Lemma 12 computes E[Z²]−(E[Z])², although complex variance requires E[|Z|²]−|E[Z]|². For x=(1,0), w=(1,1), and one counter, Z=h₁²(h₁+h₂)² has E[Z]=1, E[Z²]=2, and E[|Z|²]=6. Thus its variance is 5, while the calculation gives 1. The stated upper bound may be recoverable, but the supplied calculation does not justify the subsequent Chebyshev argument and Theorem 6.

The claimed loss of linearity in Section 4 is incorrect for the stored representation. Its counters satisfy C_(x−y)=C_x−C_y, so the median decoder can estimate weighted pairwise distances from these differences. A nonlinear decoder does not eliminate this capability. This undermines the paper's stated distinction between its two constructions and requires reconsideration of their relative advantages.

Useful compression is insufficiently established. For all-one weights, Δ=√d, making the advertised multiplicative-guarantee requirement scale as d²ε⁻²log(1/δ). Meanwhile, the experiments use inputs with only 10–100 nonzeros and sketches reaching 100,000 complex coordinates. Comparisons against exact sparse storage, including projection storage and processing costs, are needed to demonstrate practical savings. The 250-trial histograms support qualitative behavior but cannot validate the claimed tail bound or establish the Δ⁴ dependence; the distribution of nonzero input values is also unspecified.

The scope of the guarantees needs clearer qualification. Corollary 2 concerns a fixed finite collection of weights independent of the sketch randomness; it does not establish guarantees for weights chosen adaptively from previous outputs. The abstract and conclusion should also preserve the bounded-distortion condition when claiming multiplicative approximation.

Secondary presentation errors impede verification: Theorem 4 has identical 1+ε factors at both endpoints, Corollary 2 uses ∥x∥² instead of ∥x−y∥² in its upper additive error, and the closing space statement in Section 4 omits the Δ⁴ dependence. These require correction alongside the substantive proof revisions.
